text:
Remember how long thou hast already put off these things, and how
 often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the
 gods, thou hast neglected it.
plain_text: Remember how long you have been putting these things off. Again and again a moment was set before you, and again and again you let it pass.

text:
It is high time for thee to understand the
 true nature both of the world, whereof thou art a part; and of that Lord
 and Governor of the world, from whom, as a channel from the spring, thou
 thyself didst flow: and that there is but a certain limit of time
 appointed unto thee, which if thou shalt not make use of to calm and allay
 the many distempers of thy soul, it will pass away and thou with it, and
 never after return.
plain_text: It is time now to understand the true nature of the world you are part of, and of the power that governs it — the source from which you yourself flowed, like water from a spring. You have been given a limited amount of time. If you do not use it to calm the many troubles of your soul, it will pass away, and you with it, and it will never come back.

text:
Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to
 perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned
 gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other
 cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them. Which thou
 shalt do; if thou shalt go about every action as thy last action, free
 from all vanity, all passionate and wilful aberration from reason, and
 from all hypocrisy, and self-love, and dislike of those things, which by
 the fates or appointment of God have happened unto thee.
plain_text: Make it your constant care, as a person of duty, to do whatever is before you with honest seriousness, with natural kindness, with freedom, and with fairness. Let go of every other worry and distraction. You will manage this if you approach each action as though it were your last — free from all vanity, from every emotional departure from reason, from all pretending, from self-centeredness, and from resentment toward what fate has brought you.

text:
Thou seest that
 those things, which for a man to hold on in a prosperous course, and to
 live a divine life, are requisite and necessary, are not many, for the
 gods will require no more of any man, that shall but keep and observe
 these things.
plain_text: You can see that the things needed to live a good and worthy life are not many. The gods ask nothing more of anyone who keeps to these few things.

text:
Do, soul, do; abuse and contemn thyself; yet a while and the time
 for thee to respect thyself, will be at an end. Every man's happiness
 depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles
 affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in
 the souls, and conceits of other men.
plain_text: Go ahead, my soul — keep mistreating and disrespecting yourself. But soon the chance to honor yourself will be gone. Every person's happiness depends on themselves. Yet here you are, with life nearly over, still placing your happiness in the opinions and judgments of others.

text:
Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much
 distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease
 roving and wandering to and fro. Thou must also take heed of another kind
 of wandering, for they are idle in their actions, who toil and labour in
 this life, and have no certain scope to which to direct all their motions,
 and desires.
plain_text: Why should anything that happens outside of you cause so much distraction? Give yourself time to learn something worthwhile, and stop drifting from thing to thing. But watch out for another kind of wandering too. Some people are busy all their lives, working and striving, yet they have no clear purpose to guide their efforts and desires.

text:
For not observing the state of another man's soul, scarce was ever
 any man known to be unhappy. Tell whosoever they be that intend not, and
 guide not by reason and discretion the motions of their own souls, they
 must of necessity be unhappy.
plain_text: No one was ever made unhappy by failing to notice what was going on in someone else's soul. But anyone who does not pay attention to the movements of their own soul, and guide them with reason and care — that person will surely be unhappy.

text:
These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature
 of the universe, and what is mine—in particular: This unto that what
 relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And
 that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always
 both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof
 thou art a part.
plain_text: Always keep these things in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is my own nature? How does the one relate to the other? What kind of part am I, in what kind of whole? And remember that no one can stop you from doing and saying what is in harmony with the nature you belong to.

text:
Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as after a vulgar
 sense such things I grant may be compared:) says well and like a
 philosopher, that those sins are greater which are committed through lust,
 than those which are committed through anger. For he that is angry seems
 with a kind of grief and close contraction of himself, to turn away from
 reason; but he that sins through lust, being overcome by pleasure, doth in
 his very sin bewray a more impotent, and unmanlike disposition.
plain_text: Theophrastus, when comparing one wrong with another — and yes, in a general sense such things can be compared — says wisely that wrongs done out of desire are worse than wrongs done out of anger. The angry person seems to turn away from reason with a kind of pain and inner tightening. But the person who does wrong out of desire, overcome by pleasure, shows a weaker and less self-controlled character in the very act.

text:
Well then
 and like a philosopher doth he say, that he of the two is the more to be
 condemned, that sins with pleasure, than he that sins with grief. For
 indeed this latter may seem first to have been wronged, and so in some
 manner through grief thereof to have been forced to be angry, whereas he
 who through lust doth commit anything, did of himself merely resolve upon
 that action.
plain_text: He is right to say that the one who does wrong with pleasure deserves more blame than the one who does wrong with pain. After all, the angry person may have first been wronged, and so was in some way pushed into anger by grief. But the one who acts out of desire chose that action entirely on their own.

text:
Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do,
 and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very
 present depart out of this life. And as for death, if there be any gods,
 it is no grievous thing to leave the society of men. The gods will do thee
 no hurt, thou mayest be sure. But if it be so that there be no gods, or
 that they take no care of the world, why should I desire to live in a
 world void of gods, and of all divine providence?
plain_text: Whatever you do, whatever you plan, do it and plan it as someone who could leave this life at any moment. As for death — if gods exist, there is nothing terrible about leaving the company of people. The gods will not harm you, of that you can be sure. But if there are no gods, or if they do not care about the world, then why would I want to live in a world empty of gods and without any guiding hand?

text:
But gods there be
 certainly, and they take care for the world; and as for those things which
 be truly evil, as vice and wickedness, such things they have put in a
 man's own power, that he might avoid them if he would: and had there been
 anything besides that had been truly bad and evil, they would have had a
 care of that also, that a man might have avoided it. But why should that
 be thought to hurt and prejudice a man's life in this world, which cannot
 any ways make man himself the better, or the worse in his own person?
plain_text: But gods do exist, and they do care for the world. As for what is truly evil — things like vice and wickedness — they have placed those within a person's own control, so that anyone could avoid them if they chose to. And if there were anything else that was truly harmful, the gods would have made sure we could avoid that too. But how can something hurt your life if it has no power to make you a better or worse person?

text:
Neither must we think that the nature of the universe did either through
 ignorance pass these things, or if not as ignorant of them, yet as unable
 either to prevent, or better to order and dispose them. It cannot be that
 she through want either of power or skill, should have committed such a
 thing, so as to suffer all things both good and bad, equally and
 promiscuously, to happen unto all both good and bad.
plain_text: We should not think that the nature of the universe overlooked these things out of ignorance, or that it knew about them but lacked the power to prevent or arrange them better. It is not possible that nature, through any lack of power or wisdom, would have allowed good and bad things to fall equally and randomly upon good and bad people alike.

text:
As for life
 therefore, and death, honour and dishonour, labour and pleasure, riches
 and poverty, all these things happen unto men indeed, both good and bad,
 equally; but as things which of themselves are neither good nor bad;
 because of themselves, neither shameful nor praiseworthy.
plain_text: Life and death, honor and dishonor, hard work and pleasure, wealth and poverty — all of these happen equally to good and bad people alike. But these things are not good or bad in themselves. In themselves, they are neither shameful nor praiseworthy.

text:
Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the
 bodies and substances themselves, into the matter and substance of the
 world: and their memories into the general age and time of the world.
 Consider the nature of all worldly sensible things; of those especially,
 which either ensnare by pleasure, or for their irksomeness are dreadful,
 or for their outward lustre and show are in great esteem and request, how
 vile and contemptible, how base and corruptible, how destitute of all true
 life and being they are.
plain_text: Think about how quickly all things break down and dissolve — bodies returning to the raw matter of the world, and memories fading into the vast stretch of time. Think about the nature of everything we can touch and sense. Especially those things that trap us with pleasure, or fill us with dread because they are unpleasant, or impress us with their outward shine. How cheap and worthless they really are. How low and easily ruined. How empty of any true life or lasting substance.

text:
It is the part of a man endowed with a good understanding faculty, to
 consider what they themselves are in very deed, from whose bare conceits
 and voices, honour and credit do proceed: as also what it is to die, and
 how if a man shall consider this by itself alone, to die, and separate
 from it in his mind all those things which with it usually represent
 themselves unto us, he can conceive of it no otherwise, than as of a work
 of nature, and he that fears any work of nature, is a very child. Now
 death, it is not only a work of nature, but also conducing to nature.
plain_text: It is the mark of a thoughtful person to consider what kind of people those really are whose opinions give us our sense of honor and reputation. It is also wise to think about what death actually is. If you look at death on its own and strip away all the fears and images that usually surround it, you will see it as nothing more than a natural process. And anyone who fears a natural process is still a child. Death is not only something natural — it also serves nature.

text:
Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined
 unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be
 diffused.
plain_text: Think about how a person is connected to the divine, and through which part of themselves. And consider what happens to that part when it is said to spread out and lose its focus.

text:
There is nothing more wretched than that soul, which in a kind
 of circuit compasseth all things, searching (as he saith) even the very
 depths of the earth; and by all signs and conjectures prying into the very
 thoughts of other men's souls; and yet of this, is not sensible, that it
 is sufficient for a man to apply himself wholly, and to confine all his
 thoughts and cares to the tendance of that spirit which is within him, and
 truly and really to serve him.
plain_text: There is nothing more miserable than the soul that circles around everything, searching — as the saying goes — even the depths of the earth, and trying by every sign and guess to see into the thoughts of others. Yet it does not realize that it is enough to devote yourself fully to the spirit within you, and to truly serve it.

text:
His service doth consist in this, that a
 man keep himself pure from all violent passion and evil affection, from
 all rashness and vanity, and from all manner of discontent, either in
 regard of the gods or men.
plain_text: Serving that spirit means keeping yourself free from violent emotion and harmful desire, from recklessness and vanity, and from every kind of bitterness — whether toward the gods or toward other people.

text:
For indeed whatsoever proceeds from the gods,
 deserves respect for their worth and excellency; and whatsoever proceeds
 from men, as they are our kinsmen, should by us be entertained, with love,
 always; sometimes, as proceeding from their ignorance, of that which is
 truly good and bad, (a blindness no less, than that by which we are not
 able to discern between white and black:) with a kind of pity and
 compassion also.
plain_text: Whatever comes from the gods deserves respect, because of their goodness and greatness. And whatever comes from other people should be received with love, since they are our fellow human beings. Sometimes it should also be met with pity and compassion, when it comes from their inability to tell what is truly good from what is truly bad — a blindness no less real than not being able to tell white from black.

text:
If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands
 of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save
 with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he
 lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with. That
 then which is longest of duration, and that which is shortest, come both
 to one effect. For although in regard of that which is already past there
 may be some inequality, yet that time which is now present and in being,
 is equal unto all men.
plain_text: Even if you were to live three thousand years, or even ten thousand, remember this: no one can lose any life other than the one they are living right now. And the life you are living is nothing more than what you lose moment by moment. So the longest life and the shortest life amount to the same thing. The past may differ from person to person, but the present moment is equal for everyone.

text:
And that being it which we part with whensoever we
 die, it doth manifestly appear, that it can be but a moment of time, that
 we then part with. For as for that which is either past or to come, a man
 cannot be said properly to part with it. For how should a man part with
 that which he hath not? These two things therefore thou must remember.
plain_text: And since the present moment is all we lose when we die, it is clear that we only ever lose a single moment. You cannot lose the past — it is already gone. You cannot lose the future — you do not have it yet. How can you lose what you do not possess? Remember these two things.

text:
First, that all things in the world from all eternity, by a perpetual
 revolution of the same times and things ever continued and renewed, are of
 one kind and nature; so that whether for a hundred or two hundred years
 only, or for an infinite space of time, a man see those things which are
 still the same, it can be no matter of great moment.
plain_text: First, that everything in the world has been repeating in the same patterns since the beginning of time, always cycling and renewing. So whether you watch it for a hundred years, two hundred years, or forever, you are seeing the same things. The length makes no real difference.

text:
And secondly, that
 that life which any the longest liver, or the shortest liver parts with,
 is for length and duration the very same, for that only which is present,
 is that, which either of them can lose, as being that only which they
 have; for that which he hath not, no man can truly be said to lose.
plain_text: And second, that the life lost by the person who lives the longest and the life lost by the person who dies the youngest are exactly the same in length. Both can only lose the present moment, because that is all either of them truly has. No one can lose what they do not have.

text:
Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things
 are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as
 plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that
 which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is
 sweet and pleasing.
plain_text: Remember that everything comes down to opinion and belief. What was said to Monimus the Cynic makes this clear enough. And the value of that insight is just as clear — so long as you accept the hard truth in it along with what is easy and pleasant to hear.

text:
A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially,
 when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an
 excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything
 that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the
 universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are. Secondly, when she either is averse from any man, or led by contrary
 desires or affections, tending to his hurt and prejudice; such as are the
 souls of them that are angry. Thirdly, when she is overcome by any
 pleasure or pain.
plain_text: A person's soul wrongs and disrespects itself, first and most of all, when it tries to separate itself from the world like a growth cut off from the body. To be upset or displeased with anything that happens is to rebel against the nature of the universe, of which every individual nature is a part. Second, the soul wrongs itself when it turns against another person, or is driven by feelings that aim to do harm — as happens when people give in to anger. Third, when it is overcome by pleasure or pain.

text:
Fourthly, when she doth dissemble, and covertly and
 falsely either doth or saith anything. Fifthly, when she doth either
 affect or endeavour anything to no certain end, but rashly and without due
 ratiocination and consideration, how consequent or inconsequent it is to
 the common end. For even the least things ought not to be done, without
 relation unto the end; and the end of the reasonable creatures is, to
 follow and obey him, who is the reason as it were, and the law of this
 great city, and ancient commonwealth.
plain_text: Fourth, when it puts on a false face and says or does anything dishonestly or insincerely. Fifth, when it acts or strives toward no clear purpose, doing things carelessly and without thinking about whether they serve the greater good. Even the smallest actions should be done with purpose. And the purpose of all thinking beings is to follow and obey the reason and law of this great and ancient commonwealth of the universe.

text:
The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever
 flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending
 to corruption. His soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and fame doubtful;
 to be brief, as a stream so are all things belonging to the body; as a
 dream, or as a smoke, so are all that belong unto the soul. Our life is a
 warfare, and a mere pilgrimage. Fame after life is no better than
 oblivion. What is it then that will adhere and follow? Only one thing,
 philosophy.
plain_text: A person's time on earth is just a point. The body is always changing. The senses are dim. The whole body moves toward decay. The soul is restless. Fortune is uncertain. Fame is unreliable. In short — everything about the body flows like a stream, and everything about the soul drifts like a dream or fades like smoke. Life is a struggle and a journey through a strange land. Fame after death is no better than being forgotten. What, then, will stay with you? Only one thing: philosophy.

text:
And philosophy doth consist in this, for a man to preserve
 that spirit which is within him, from all manner of contumelies and
 injuries, and above all pains or pleasures; never to do anything either
 rashly, or feignedly, or hypocritically: wholly to depend from himself and
 his own proper actions: all things that happen unto him to embrace
 contentedly, as coming from Him from whom he himself also came; and above
 all things, with all meekness and a calm cheerfulness, to expect death, as
 being nothing else but the resolution of those elements, of which every
 creature is composed.
plain_text: And philosophy means this: to protect the spirit within you from all insults and harm, and above all from being ruled by pain or pleasure. Never to act carelessly, or falsely, or with pretense. To depend entirely on yourself and your own actions. To accept everything that happens with contentment, knowing it comes from the same source you came from. And above all, to await death with gentleness and quiet calm — seeing it as nothing more than the breaking apart of the elements that every living thing is made of.

text:
And if the elements themselves suffer nothing by
 this their perpetual conversion of one into another, that dissolution, and
 alteration, which is so common unto all, why should it be feared by any? Is not this according to nature? But nothing that is according to nature
 can be evil. Whilst I was at Carnuntum.
plain_text: If the elements themselves are not harmed by their constant changing from one form to another — this dissolving and reshaping that happens to everything — then why should anyone fear it? Is it not simply nature at work? And nothing that follows nature can be evil. Written while I was at Carnuntum.
